questions.mini_lesson: Effective habitat management requires reading local context rather than applying cookie-cutter rules: Dachigam and Kedarnath are both fragile, short-season Himalayan alpine meadows, yet Kedarnath must manage intense pilgrimage foot traffic along sacred routes; similarly, thorny scrub in Ranthambore may be either a healthy, natural semi-arid ecosystem for ungulates and tigers or a once-dense forest degraded by overgrazing and lopping. Option (C) makes the classic mistake of dismissing natural scrub.

questions.question: Why are the Spiny-tailed lizard in Rajasthan's Thar desert and flamingos in Gujarat's Little Rann of Kutch vulnerable even when their broad regional landscapes still exist on maps?
options: Because both species require dense coniferous snow forests to survive
Because Spiny-tailed lizards are marine filter feeders and flamingos burrow in dry sand dunes

Because they depend on narrow microhabitat conditions - the Spiny-tailed lizard requires undisturbed sandy soil for burrows to escape desert heat and predators, while flamingos require a tight window of shallow water depth and salinity to filter-feed on algae and plankton
Because both species are invasive generalists that thrive on vehicle compaction and industrial brine dumping
questions.transcript_quote: The spiny-tailed lizard illustrates a broad ecological principle here. Many species depend not just on a general habitat type, but on specific microclimates within it. This lizard uses burrows for protection from heat and predators... It requires undisturbed sandy soil for burrowing... Flamingos depend on shallow saline wetlands and mud flats... Habitat suitability in such places is controlled primarily by water depth and salinity. If conditions move outside a narrow range, effective feeding becomes impossible.
questions.mini_lesson: Broad biome labels ('desert' or 'wetland') hide critical microhabitat requirements: in Jodhpur's arid plains, surface disturbance by tractors, vehicles, or solar/wind grading crushes the burrows that Spiny-tailed lizards need for thermoregulation and predator escape; in the Little Rann of Kutch (also home to the Indian wild ass), water diversion or salt-pan changes that alter depth or salinity outside a narrow band prevent congregating flamingos from filter-feeding. Option (B) swaps the two species' adaptations.

questions.question: Which pairing accurately describes the ecological features of Chilika Lake, Western Ghats Shola-grassland mosaics, and coastal mangroves?
options: Chilika is an alpine glacier in Kashmir, Sholas are arid salt flats in Gujarat, and mangroves are deep-sea trenches
Chilika contains only pure freshwater with zero marine connection, Sholas are single-species eucalyptus plantations, and mangroves lack roots
All three habitats are artificial urban reservoirs created in the late 20th century

Chilika is India's largest brackish coastal lagoon (a Ramsar site in Odisha supporting the rare Irrawaddy dolphin), Shola-grasslands are high-elevation valley-forest and ridge-grassland mosaics that sustain peninsular rivers, and mangroves use prop roots and gas-exchanging pneumatophores in intertidal mudflats
questions.transcript_quote: Chilika lake in Odisha is India's largest coastal lagoon and a Ramsar wetland of international importance... Chilika supports fish populations, migratory birds and the globally rare Irrawaddy dolphin... Shola forests are montane forest-grassland mosaics found in the higher elevations of the Western Ghats... Mangroves occupy the intertidal zone... They survive waterlogged saline conditions through structural adaptations: prop roots for support and pneumatophores projecting above the water line for gas exchange.
questions.mini_lesson: Lecture 29 highlights three signature Indian wetland/forest systems: (1) Chilika Lake in Odisha, where freshwater river inflow and seawater mixing create a productive brackish Ramsar lagoon for migratory waterfowl and Irrawaddy dolphins; (2) Western Ghats Shola-grasslands, an integrated unit of stunted evergreen forest in misty valley folds and grasslands on ridges that regulates river flows; and (3) intertidal mangroves equipped with structural prop roots and upward-breathing pneumatophores. Options (A), (B), and (C) misstate their geography and ecology.

questions.question: What is the difference between *de jure* protection and *de facto* habitat conditions, and when does a habitat become an 'ecological trap'?
options: *De jure* refers to legal designation on paper and maps, whereas *de facto* refers to actual on-the-ground conditions (food, water, shelter, breeding sites, low disturbance); when degradation erodes *de facto* conditions, a habitat that still looks suitable on paper can lure animals into an ecological trap where survival or reproduction fails
*De jure* refers to soil nutrient chemistry, whereas *de facto* refers only to international treaties
A legally notified sanctuary automatically guarantees 100% reproductive success regardless of sand mining or pollution
An ecological trap is a steel cage used by researchers during focal animal sampling
questions.transcript_quote: Habitat quality depends on the real on the ground availability of food, water, shelter, breeding sites and freedom from disturbance. These are what we call de facto conditions - the conditions on the ground. When disturbance and degradation erode these conditions, a habitat can become an ecological trap - a place that appears suitable but cannot sustain survival or reproduction... The core insight is the gap between de jure protection - what the law designates - and de facto conditions - what is actually happening on the ground.
questions.mini_lesson: Conservation law creates *de jure* protected areas on maps, but wild animals survive and breed only if *de facto* conditions on the ground remain intact; when human pressures degrade nesting banks or water quality inside a park that still looks physically present, animals drawn to the site suffer reproductive failure or high mortality - turning the habitat into an ecological trap. Option (C) is the 'paper park' fallacy refuted throughout Lecture 29.

questions.question: In the National Chambal Sanctuary case study, how do multiple human pressures combine to degrade *de facto* habitat quality for the Critically Endangered Gharial?
options: Only a single pressure - natural monsoon rain - affects the Chambal River

Large-scale mechanical sand mining (documented via satellite imagery in Morena) physically removes nesting sandbars, while riverside farming, noisy water pumps, fertilizer/pesticide runoff, cattle trampling, and river barrages cumulatively make the sanctuary inhospitable for natural breeding
Sand mining improves gharial nesting by excavating deep vertical pits in the riverbank
Field foot patrols alone easily detect 100% of illegal sand extraction without any need for satellite remote sensing
questions.transcript_quote: Spatial analysis reveals near complete coverage of usable nesting banks by sand mining activity... Beyond direct physical destruction, the habitat faces cumulative degradation from multiple sources: agricultural fields extend to the very edge of the riverbank... water extraction pumps for agriculture create continuous noise and smoke... fertilizers, pesticides, and other chemicals drain directly from fields into the river... cattle grazing compacts soil and sand... barrages and dams fragment the river.
questions.mini_lesson: The Chambal Gharial study is a masterclass in cumulative impact assessment and remote sensing: satellite imagery revealed dozens of excavators stripping away specific sloped sandbars in Morena district on a scale invisible to routine foot patrols, while riverside farming, noisy diesel pumps, agrochemical runoff tainting fish prey, livestock bank compaction, washing disturbance, and dams jointly pushed *de facto* habitat quality below the breeding threshold. Options (C) and (D) reverse the findings.

questions.question: What does the reliance on *ex-situ* egg collection, hatchery incubation, and juvenile rearing ('head-starting') for Gharials inside the National Chambal Sanctuary signify?
options: That gharials have evolved to lay eggs only inside concrete incubators and never in river sand
That *in-situ* habitat conditions in the Chambal River are completely pristine and undisturbed

That *de facto* nesting conditions inside a legally designated sanctuary have deteriorated so severely from sand mining and disturbance that natural *in-situ* hatching cannot sustain the population without *ex-situ* intervention
That legal sanctuary designation on paper is sufficient by itself to prevent local extinction
questions.transcript_quote: For gharials in Chambal, however, degradation has progressed to the point where ex-situ elements have also become necessary: collecting eggs from vulnerable nests, hatching them in a protected offsite facility, rearing hatchlings to a more robust life stage, and then releasing them back into the sanctuary. That this step is required inside a legally designated protected area is a clear indicator that de facto conditions have fallen below the threshold that is needed for natural breeding.
questions.mini_lesson: Normally, inside a vast national wildlife sanctuary, *in-situ* protection should allow wild species to breed naturally; the fact that managers must collect wild Gharial eggs from Chambal sandbars, hatch them in offsite hatcheries, rear juveniles until large enough to survive, and release them back proves that *de facto* riverine habitat quality has dropped below the threshold required for natural recruitment. Options (B) and (D) ignore the lesson of the case study.

questions.question: How does 'behavioural ecology' differ from classical 'ethology', and how is the cost-benefit framework illustrated by group living in lions?
options: Ethology describes and catalogs observable behaviour in natural settings, whereas behavioural ecology examines how behaviours evolve through fitness cost-benefit trade-offs - such as male lions in coalitions gaining pride access and cub defense at the cost of shared paternity, while females gain cooperative territory defense at the cost of within-group food competition
Ethology studies only plant root chemistry, whereas behavioural ecology studies only fossilized dinosaur bones
Group living in lions carries only benefits and zero costs, and those benefits are identical for males and females
Natural selection favours behaviours whenever their energetic and injury cost exceeds their survival and reproductive benefit
questions.transcript_quote: Ethology is the scientific study of animal behavior, typically through systematic observation in natural settings. It focuses on describing and cataloging what animals do. Behavioral ecology goes a step further by asking why those behaviors exist... Males in a coalition gain access to mates and can collectively defend cubs from infanticide. Their cost is that paternity must be shared among coalition members. Females benefit from kin support and cooperative territory defense helping to secure food. The cost is that within-group competition can reduce each individual's food intake.
questions.mini_lesson: Ethology asks *what* animals do (observing and cataloging natural behaviours), whereas behavioural ecology asks *why* natural selection favours a behaviour using cost-benefit economics (benefit $>$ cost): in lions, group living pays off differently by sex - male coalitions trade shared paternity for pride takeover and cub survival, while female prides trade increased food competition/parasite risk for cooperative hunting, cub defense, and territory retention. Options (C) and (D) violate cost-benefit selection logic.

questions.question: According to W. D. Hamilton's rule ($r \cdot b > c$) and J. B. S. Haldane's inclusive fitness illustration, when is a costly helping or alarm-calling behaviour evolutionarily favoured?
options: Only when the genetic relatedness ($r$) between helper and recipient is zero

When genetic relatedness ($r$) multiplied by the reproductive benefit to the relative ($b$) exceeds the reproductive cost to the helper ($c$) - which is why sacrificing oneself can preserve equivalent shared genes if it saves more than 2 siblings ($r = 0.50$), 4 nephews/nieces ($r = 0.25$), or 8 cousins ($r = 0.125$)
When the personal cost to the actor ($c$) is ten times larger than the benefit to the relative ($b$)
Only when animals act for the good of unrelated species through group selection regardless of genetic relatedness
questions.transcript_quote: Hamilton's rule states that a helping behavior is favored by natural selection when relatedness multiplied by the benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost to the helper, written as r into b greater than c... If an individual loses its life to save two of its siblings or four nephews or nieces or eight cousins, then this can be a fair deal in evolutionary terms. Siblings share approximately 50% of genes, nephews and nieces 25% and cousins 12.5%.
questions.mini_lesson: Kin selection explains apparent altruism (such as ground squirrel alarm calls or cooperative breeding) through indirect/inclusive fitness: because relatives share alleles by common descent ($r = 0.5$ for full siblings, $0.25$ for nephews/nieces, $0.125$ for first cousins), natural selection favours a helping gene whenever $r \cdot b > c$, famously summarized by Haldane's remark that he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins. Options (A), (C), and (D) invert Hamilton's inequality.

questions.question: What are the four categories of territorial defence strategies, and how does territory size respond to changes in food resource density (such as flower density for nectar-feeding hummingbirds)?
options: Territorial defence uses only lethal physical combat, and territory size expands when flower density increases
Territory size is a rigid, unchanging genetic constant for every species regardless of food abundance

Animals defend territories using auditory (calls/roars), visual (displays/postures), olfactory (scent marking), and physical (chasing/fighting) strategies, and territory size decreases inversely as resource density increases because energy needs can be met in a smaller area
Olfactory scent marking works only when the territory owner is physically standing on the boundary
questions.transcript_quote: Territorial defense strategies fall into four categories: auditory defense... visual defense... olfactory defense employs scent marking, urine, or gland secretions that advertise occupancy even when the animal is absent... physical defense escalates to chasing, fighting, or ritualized aggression... As flower density increases, more food is available in a concentrated manner, and the territory size decreases, since an animal can now meet its energy needs from a smaller area.
questions.mini_lesson: Because physical combat (as in chital, blackbuck, rhinos, or colonial penguins) risks serious injury, animals escalate territorial defense from low-cost auditory calls, visual postures, and persistent olfactory scent marks up to physical fights only when necessary; moreover, territory size is plastic and inversely proportional to resource density - when nectar-rich flowers are dense, a hummingbird defends a much smaller patch than when flowers are sparse. Options (A), (B), and (D) contradict these behavioural principles.

questions.question: In the camera-trap 24-hour activity study from Sariska Tiger Reserve, what did the temporal overlap coefficients between tiger-chital ($0.24$) and tiger-jackal ($0.67$) indicate?
options: That chital deer actively hunt tigers during the middle of the night
That camera-trap activity curves alone prove with 100% certainty the exact physiological cause of every interaction without needing field context
That tigers and chital have identical 24-hour activity schedules ($1.00$), whereas jackals never use the same forest

That the prey species (chital) showed low temporal overlap ($0.24$) with the tiger - consistent with temporal predator avoidance - whereas the scavenger (jackal) showed much higher temporal overlap ($0.67$), consistent with scavenging on tiger kills or shared habitat timing
questions.transcript_quote: In this activity plot, we observe an overlap coefficient of 0.24 between tiger and chital in Sariska, representing low overlap between activity patterns in this predator-prey relationship. In contrast, we observe a much higher overlap coefficient of 0.67 between tiger and jackal in Sariska, representing higher overlap between activity patterns in this predator-scavenger relationship.
questions.mini_lesson: By plotting time-stamped camera-trap detections across a 24-hour clock, ecologists quantify how species partition time: in Sariska, chital deer minimized activity during peak tiger hours (low overlap of $0.24$, suggesting temporal anti-predator avoidance), whereas golden jackals matched tiger activity windows closely (high overlap of $0.67$, reflecting scavenging opportunities on tiger kills), though field context is always required to confirm the mechanism. Option (B) ignores the lecture's caution that activity curves generate hypotheses rather than standalone proof.

questions.question: In a standardized ungulate ethogram, how is the trade-off between 'vigilance' and 'feeding' defined, and how is 'auto-grooming' distinguished from 'allo-grooming'?
options: Vigilance and feeding can both be performed simultaneously at 100% capacity, and auto-grooming means fighting with predators

Vigilance (stationary with ears raised scanning surroundings) trades off against feeding (mouth directed at vegetation consuming food), while auto-grooming is self-scratching/licking to remove ectoparasites and allo-grooming is one individual grooming another to strengthen social bonds
Walking is defined as having all four hooves suspended in the air, whereas running requires the abdomen touching the ground
Ethogram definitions are intentionally vague so each observer can invent personal categories in the field
questions.transcript_quote: Vigilance is defined as the animal stationary, ears raised, and actively scanning the surroundings... Increased vigilance typically comes at the cost of reduced feeding time since both cannot be performed simultaneously at full capacity... Auto grooming is defined as an animal scratching or licking its own body. It helps remove ectoparasites, irritants, and debris... Allo grooming is defined as one animal grooming another individual. It can strengthen social bonds, reduce mutual parasite loads, or signal tolerance or kinship.
questions.mini_lesson: An ethogram eliminates observer bias by defining mutually clear, repeatable behaviour states: because an ungulate cannot keep its head down cropping grass (feeding) while holding its head up with ears raised scanning for predators (vigilance), rising disturbance or predator risk forces a measurable drop in feeding time; similarly, ethograms separate self-maintenance (auto-grooming) from social bonding (allo-grooming), and slow locomotion with at least one hoof grounded (walking) from aerial suspension phases (running). Option (C) swaps walking, running, and sitting.

questions.question: How does 'scan sampling' differ from 'focal animal sampling' when constructing a time budget, and why did juvenile chital show lower vigilance than adults in the Lecture 30 field study?
options: Scan sampling follows a single animal continuously for hours, whereas focal sampling photographs the entire forest once a year
Juveniles showed 100% vigilance and zero feeding because young animals do not need energy for growth
Scan sampling never misses brief 1-second behaviours between intervals, and focal sampling never depends on which individual is chosen

Scan sampling records the current activity of all visible group members at regular intervals (efficient for group patterns, though brief behaviours between scans may be missed), whereas focal sampling follows one individual continuously to record exact durations; in the time budget, juveniles showed lower vigilance because group protection allowed them to prioritize feeding during active growth
questions.transcript_quote: Scan sampling records the behavior of all visible individuals at set regular intervals... Its main limitation, however, is that brief behaviors occurring between the scan intervals may be missed... Focal animal sampling: a single individual is selected and is followed continuously for a fixed period... Juveniles showed lower vigilance than adults, possibly because group members provide collective protection that reduces individual vigilance requirement for young animals who also need to concentrate more on feeding being in the active growth phases.
questions.mini_lesson: Field ethologists use two complementary sampling protocols to build percentage time budgets: *scan sampling* sweeps left-to-right across a herd at fixed time ticks to capture group-level activity (trading off missed brief events between scans), while *focal animal sampling* tracks one unbiasedly chosen individual continuously to log exact start/end durations and sequences. In the chital time-budget analysis, feeding, walking, and looking dominated overall, with juveniles investing less time in vigilance and more in feeding thanks to the collective safety shield of adult herd members. Options (A), (B), and (C) reverse the methods and findings.

questions.question: Which species concept defines species mainly by niche, resources, and environmental conditions used?
options: Evolutionary species concept
Ecological species concept
Biological species concept
Morphological species concept
questions.transcript_quote: The ecological species concept defines species by niche, the resources and conditions that the species use.
questions.mini_lesson: The Ecological Species Concept defines a species by its functional role (ecological niche) in the environment - the specific food resources, microhabitat, and environmental conditions it exploits (such as canopy feeder vs. ground detritivore). Option (A) focuses on independent ancestor-descendant lineage fate, Option (C) focuses on interbreeding and reproductive isolation, and Option (D) focuses on visible anatomical traits.

questions.question: Habitat quality depends mainly on:
options: Legal status alone
Whether the habitat appears on a map
Food, water, shelter, breeding sites, and low disturbance
Whether only one species is present
questions.transcript_quote: Habitat quality depends on the real on the ground availability of food, water, shelter, breeding sites and freedom from disturbance. These are what we call de facto conditions.
questions.mini_lesson: Wild animals respond to *de facto* (on-the-ground) ecological conditions - whether they can find sufficient food, clean water, protective cover, intact breeding/nesting substrates, and low human disturbance - rather than *de jure* legal notifications on paper. Options (A) and (B) represent the 'paper park' fallacy exposed by the National Chambal Sanctuary gharial case study.

questions.question: Genetic diversity refers to:
options: Variation in hereditary information among individuals and populations
Difference in species composition between two ecosystems
Number of habitats across a landscape
Number of visible traits in a field guide
questions.transcript_quote: Genetic diversity is the variation in the hereditary information carried by individuals within a species. It occurs at the level of genes, alleles, and chromosomes. And it varies both among individuals within a population and between populations of the same species.
questions.mini_lesson: Genetic diversity is the foundational level of the biodiversity pyramid, measuring heritable variation in DNA sequences, alleles, and chromosomes both among individuals within a population and between different populations of the same species. Option (B) defines beta diversity (species turnover), and Option (C) defines ecosystem diversity.

questions.question: A biodiversity hotspot combines which three features?
options: High rainfall, high elevation, and high productivity
High abundance, low disturbance, and uniform habitat
High genetic similarity, low endemism, and low threat
High species richness, high endemism, and significant threat
questions.transcript_quote: A biodiversity hotspot is a region that combines three criteria: exceptionally high species richness, high levels of endemism, meaning many different species that are found nowhere else, and significant threat from human activity.
questions.mini_lesson: To qualify as a biodiversity hotspot (such as the Western Ghats or Eastern Himalayas), a region must combine high overall species richness with high endemism ($\ge 1,500$ endemic vascular plant species found nowhere else) and severe habitat threat ($\ge 70\%$ loss of original primary vegetation). Option (A) lists physical geographic features, while Options (B) and (C) invert threat and endemism into 'low disturbance' and 'low endemism'.

questions.question: Which barrier acts before fertilization?
options: Hybrid sterility
Hybrid breakdown
Embryo inviability
Temporal isolation
questions.transcript_quote: Prezygotic barriers act before fertilization preventing mating or preventing gametes from joining... Temporal isolation means breeding seasons do not overlap.
questions.mini_lesson: Reproductive isolating barriers are split at the moment of fertilization (zygote formation): pre-zygotic barriers - habitat, temporal, behavioural, mechanical, and gametic isolation - act *before* fertilization to prevent mating or gamete fusion, whereas Options (A), (B), and (C) are all post-zygotic barriers that act *after* a hybrid zygote has already formed.

questions.question: Allelopathy occurs when:
options: Animals form groups to avoid predators
One organism releases chemicals that inhibit another
Species shift upward in altitude because of warming
Adjacent populations interbreed around a barrier
questions.transcript_quote: Allelopathy is the suppression of one organism by chemicals released by another.
questions.mini_lesson: Allelopathy is a biotic interaction where a plant, fungus, or microbe releases biochemical compounds (through leaves, roots, or decaying litter, as seen in sparse undergrowth beneath teak trees or fungal antibiosis in petri dishes) that suppress the germination or root growth of competing species. Option (A) describes anti-predator social grouping, Option (C) describes altitudinal range shift, and Option (D) describes a ring species.

questions.question: Gamma diversity refers to:
options: Diversity within one wetland
Total diversity across a larger region
Evenness of individuals among species
Fitness differences between populations
questions.transcript_quote: Gamma diversity is the total biodiversity across an entire region, encompassing all the sites within it.
questions.mini_lesson: In Whittaker's spatial scale framework, Alpha ($\alpha$) diversity is local diversity within a single site (like one wetland in Option A), Beta ($\beta$) diversity is compositional difference between sites, and Gamma ($\gamma$) diversity is the total combined species diversity across an entire region or landscape. Option (C) defines species evenness.

questions.question: What does biodiversity mean?
options: Only the number of large animals in a forest
Only the number of protected areas in a landscape
Only variation in climate and soil
The variety of life within species, among species, and among ecosystems
questions.transcript_quote: Biodiversity means the variety of life... It includes diversity within species, meaning genetic variation among individuals. It includes diversity among species, meaning the range of distinct species in an area. And it includes diversity among ecosystems, meaning the variety of habitat types and the ecological processes that they support.
questions.mini_lesson: Biological diversity encompasses the full three-tiered hierarchy of living variation: genetic diversity (within species), species diversity (among all species including plants, fungi, and microbes, not just charismatic megafauna), and ecosystem diversity (among habitats and ecological processes). Options (A), (B), and (C) use restrictive 'Only' traps that reduce biodiversity to megafauna, administrative parks, or abiotic factors.

questions.question: What is speciation?
options: The seasonal movement of individuals between habitats
The increase in population size within one area
The grouping of organisms according to body colour
The splitting of one lineage into two or more independently evolving species
questions.transcript_quote: Speciation is the term used for the process by which one ancestral lineage splits into two or more independently evolving species.
questions.mini_lesson: Speciation is the evolutionary branching process where reduced gene flow between subpopulations allows independent genetic divergence (via mutation, natural selection, and drift) to build reproductive barriers, splitting one ancestral lineage into two or more distinct species. Option (A) defines seasonal migration, Option (B) defines population growth, and Option (C) describes superficial sorting.

questions.question: Which idea best describes a species as a scientific concept?
options: A fixed sentence that applies equally to every organism
A category based only on visible form
A flexible tool that may emphasize interbreeding, form, ancestry, or niche
A group that must always be geographically isolated
questions.transcript_quote: Because different frameworks emphasize different aspects - interbreeding, form, ancestry or niche - species is best understood as a flexible scientific tool rather than one fixed definition.
questions.mini_lesson: Because no single species definition works flawlessly across sexual animals, asexual bacteria, ancient fossils, cryptic lineages, and hybrid zones, scientists use 'species' as an integrative, flexible conceptual toolkit that draws on reproductive gene flow, morphology, phylogenetic ancestry, and ecological niche depending on the organism and conservation question. Options (A), (B), and (D) rely on rigid absolutes ('fixed', 'only', 'always').

questions.question: In wildlife monitoring, how does relative abundance differ from absolute abundance?
options: Relative abundance counts every single organism in the biosphere, whereas absolute abundance measures only plants

Relative abundance uses an indirect proxy index (such as encounter rate or dung piles per kilometre) to track trends, whereas absolute abundance estimates the actual total number of individuals in an area
Relative abundance requires capturing and marking all individuals, whereas absolute abundance uses only roadside sightings
Relative abundance is always free from observer bias, whereas absolute abundance is always biased
questions.transcript_quote: Absolute abundance refers to the actual total number of individual organisms present in a defined area, whereas relative abundance provides an index or proxy metric - such as encounter rates, vocalization counts, or dung piles per kilometre - used to compare habitats or track trends over time.
questions.mini_lesson: Counting or estimating the exact headcount of elusive forest animals (absolute abundance) is often prohibitively expensive or impossible. When managers primarily need to know whether a population is increasing, stable, or declining across years, they use relative abundance indices (such as tracks or dung piles per km walked) under standardized conditions. Distractor (D) uses the false absolute 'always'.

questions.question: Using the basic population balancing equation $N_{t+1} = N_t + (B + I) - (D + E)$, what will the population size $N_{t+1}$ be if an initial deer population of $N_t = 300$ experiences $50$ births, $20$ immigrants, $35$ deaths, and $15$ emigrants over one year?
options: 280 individuals
300 individuals
320 individuals
420 individuals
questions.transcript_quote: The basic population balancing equation is $N_{t+1} = N_t + (B + I) - (D + E)$, where births ($B$) and immigration ($I$) are added as demographic gains, and deaths ($D$) and emigration ($E$) are subtracted as demographic losses.
questions.mini_lesson: To find the next year's population size $N_{t+1}$, add the demographic gains $(B + I = 50 + 20 = 70)$ to the starting population $(300 + 70 = 370)$, and subtract the demographic losses $(D + E = 35 + 15 = 50)$, giving $370 - 50 = 320$ individuals. Distractor (A) reverses gains and losses ($300 - 70 + 50 = 280$), while (D) adds losses instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: Why is a complete census (total count of every individual) rarely feasible in most wildlife studies?
options: Wild animals are often cryptic, mobile, and distributed across vast or dense habitats where some individuals inevitably remain undetected
Ecological laws prohibit counting more than ten individuals per protected area
Complete censuses can only be performed on microbial soil organisms
Counting all individuals automatically causes genetic drift in the population
questions.transcript_quote: In most wildlife studies, a complete census - counting every single individual in the population - is impossible because wild animals move, hide in dense vegetation, and occupy large landscapes, resulting in imperfect detection.
questions.mini_lesson: Unlike stationary trees in a small plot, free-ranging wild animals flee, hide in burrows or thickets, or move across boundaries during a count, making $100\%$ detection across an entire reserve practically impossible. Consequently, wildlife science relies on rigorous sampling designs and detection-corrected statistical estimators rather than raw total counts. Distractor (C) is backwards (microbes are even harder to census completely).

questions.question: In demographic modelling, what defines a “closed population” during a short-term wildlife survey?
options: A population kept permanently inside an indoor zoo enclosure
A population that experiences no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration during the survey period
A population in which all individuals have identical genotypes
A population that never interacts with any other species in its community
questions.transcript_quote: A closed population is one in which the population size remains constant during the short duration of the study, assuming no demographic additions (births or immigration) and no demographic losses (deaths or emigration).
questions.mini_lesson: In capture-recapture and abundance estimation, the 'closure assumption' means the population neither gains nor loses members while the survey is underway ($B = I = D = E = 0$). Researchers satisfy this assumption in the field by keeping trapping sessions short (e.g., a few days or weeks outside the breeding and migration seasons). Distractor (A) confuses mathematical demographic closure with physical captivity.

questions.question: What is the distinction between crude density and ecological density?
options: Crude density measures only juvenile animals, whereas ecological density measures only breeding adults
Crude density includes all species in a biome, whereas ecological density includes only invasive species
Crude density is calculated using satellites, whereas ecological density is calculated using pitfall traps
Crude density is the number of individuals per unit of total geographic area, whereas ecological density is the number of individuals per unit of actually suitable or habitable area
questions.transcript_quote: Crude density divides the total population size by the entire geographic area of the reserve, whereas ecological density divides the population size only by the area of suitable, usable habitat actually available to that species.
questions.mini_lesson: A 500 $\text{km}^2$ sanctuary might contain 100 $\text{km}^2$ of barren rock and deep reservoirs that a forest-floor herbivore can never use. Dividing the population by all 500 $\text{km}^2$ gives crude density, whereas dividing by the 400 $\text{km}^2$ of actually usable forest gives ecological density - a much more realistic measure of crowding and resource competition.

questions.question: For a relative abundance index (such as call counts per hour or track counts per kilometre) to reliably reflect population changes across years, which condition is essential?
options: The habitat type and weather conditions must be changed deliberately each year
Every single animal in the reserve must be physically captured and weighed
The survey protocol, season, and detection conditions must be standardized so the index remains proportional to true abundance
Only untrained volunteers must be used so that search effort varies randomly
questions.transcript_quote: A relative abundance index is useful for monitoring temporal trends only when survey effort, season, time of day, and detection conditions are strictly standardized so that changes in the index reflect real changes in population size rather than changes in detectability.
questions.mini_lesson: If you count bird calls at dawn in spring one year and at noon during a monsoon storm the next year, your count will drop even if the bird population doubled. Therefore, relative abundance indices require strict standardization of field effort, timing, and visibility so the proportionality between the index and actual population size stays constant. Distractor (A) would destroy index comparability.

questions.question: In ecological measurement and wildlife monitoring, what does “accuracy” refer to?
options: The closeness of a measured or estimated value to the actual, true underlying population value
The degree of clustering among repeated measurements regardless of whether they are near the true value
The total number of decimal places displayed on a digital measuring instrument
The speed at which field observers walk along a transect line
questions.transcript_quote: Accuracy (or correctness) refers to how close a measured or estimated value is to the actual, true underlying population parameter.
questions.mini_lesson: In wildlife statistics, accuracy means hitting the bullseye - getting an estimate that is centred on the true population value without systematic distortion. Distractor (B) is the classic sibling-term swap: it defines 'precision' (repeatability or tight clustering of repeated measurements), while (C) confuses instrument resolution with accuracy.

questions.question: What does “precision” (repeatability) mean in wildlife survey statistics?
options: The complete absence of any equipment calibration error
The degree of mutual agreement, closeness, or clustering among repeated independent measurements of the same quantity
The ratio of sampled compartments to total forest compartments
The ability to census 100% of a population without taking samples
questions.transcript_quote: Precision (or repeatability) is the degree of mutual agreement, closeness, or tight clustering among repeated independent measurements of the same quantity under identical conditions, reflecting low random variance.
questions.mini_lesson: Precision measures how consistent and repeatable your survey estimates are when you repeat the sampling process - in other words, how tightly your shots cluster together on a target (low variance / narrow confidence intervals). Distractor (A) describes freedom from equipment bias (accuracy), while (C) defines sampling intensity.

questions.question: A faulty laser rangefinder consistently adds exactly $15\text{ metres}$ to every sighting distance, producing nearly identical readings of $65.1\text{ m}$, $65.0\text{ m}$, and $65.1\text{ m}$ for a tree that is actually $50.0\text{ m}$ away. How are these measurements classified?
options: High accuracy and high precision
High accuracy but low precision
High precision but low accuracy (systematically biased)
Low precision and zero systematic bias
questions.transcript_quote: A survey method or instrument can be highly precise yet completely inaccurate: for example, an uncalibrated rangefinder that yields nearly identical repeated measurements that are all systematically shifted away from the true distance.
questions.mini_lesson: Because the three readings ($65.1, 65.0, 65.1\text{ m}$) cluster extremely tightly together, the instrument has high precision (repeatability). However, because all three readings are systematically shifted $15\text{ m}$ away from the true value of $50.0\text{ m}$ due to faulty calibration, the measurements have low accuracy (high equipment bias). Distractor (A) confuses tight clustering with truth.

questions.question: Systematic differences in animal detection caused by variations in field staff visual acuity, hearing ability, experience level, or fatigue are known as:
options: Equipment bias
Random sampling intensity
Probability proportional to size bias
Observer bias
questions.transcript_quote: Observer bias arises from systematic differences in detection, species identification, or counting caused by variations in observer visual acuity, hearing thresholds, field experience, alertness, or fatigue.
questions.mini_lesson: When a veteran tracker spots twice as many camouflaged deer or hears high-pitched bird calls that a tired novice misses, the resulting distortion in survey data is observer bias. Field managers reduce observer bias through standardized training, joint calibration walks, observer rotation, and double-observer protocols. Distractor (A) refers to mechanical/electronic instrument failure.

questions.question: If a wildlife survey design suffers from severe systematic bias (such as surveying only beside artificial waterholes during the dry season), what happens if you simply double the number of days spent counting at those same waterholes?
options: The systematic bias automatically disappears and the estimate becomes completely accurate
Precision increases around the wrong value, leaving the estimate systematically biased
Both precision and accuracy drop to zero
The survey automatically converts into a simple random sample
questions.transcript_quote: Increasing sample size at unrepresentative sites reduces random scatter (improving precision), but it cannot eliminate systematic sampling bias; it merely produces a more precise estimate of the wrong value.
questions.mini_lesson: Larger sample sizes shrink random error (standard error), making your confidence intervals narrower and your estimate more precise. However, if your sampling locations are fundamentally unrepresentative (convenience/waterhole bias), collecting more data at those same biased spots only locks you more tightly onto a systematically inflated number! Distractor (A) is a common statistical misconception.

questions.question: A reserve contains $200$ forest compartments of equal size, and a monitoring team surveys $30$ of these compartments. What is the sampling intensity?
questions.transcript_quote: Sampling intensity is calculated as the number of sample units surveyed ($n$) divided by the total number of population units in the study universe ($N$): $\text{Sampling Intensity} = n / N$.
questions.mini_lesson: Applying the sampling intensity formula $\text{Sampling Intensity} = n / N = 30 / 200 = 0.15$, or $15\%$. Distractor (B) confuses the raw count of sampled units ($n = 30$) with the percentage intensity ($15\%$), while (A) inverts the fraction ($200 / 30$).

questions.question: Which monitoring technology is specifically suited for surveying deep-diving cetaceans (whales and dolphins) and nocturnal echolocating bats that are difficult to observe visually?
options: Coloured UV pan trapping
Pugmark Impression Pads (PIPs)
Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM)
Herbarium pressing
questions.transcript_quote: Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) uses automated underwater hydrophones or terrestrial ultrasonic recorders to continuously capture vocalizations and echolocation clicks of deep-diving cetaceans, nocturnal bats, and cryptic birds.
questions.mini_lesson: Marine mammals spend most of their lives underwater out of sight, and micro-bats fly in complete darkness, but both rely heavily on sound (songs, clicks, and ultrasonic echolocation) to navigate and communicate. Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) deploys moored hydrophones or acoustic loggers to detect species presence and activity non-invasively 24 hours a day. The distractors apply to insects (A), terrestrial carnivore footprints (B), and dried plant specimens (D).

questions.question: Why did Indian wildlife agencies largely transition away from the historical Pugmark Census Method toward camera-trap mark-recapture for estimating tiger numbers?
options: Tigers stopped walking on forest trails after the year 2000
Pugmark shapes vary with soil substrate, gait, and observer tracing skill, creating high subjective bias and unreliable individual identification
Camera traps require no batteries or field deployment
Pugmarks can only be recorded for arboreal primates
questions.transcript_quote: The historical Pugmark Census Method - recording plaster casts and tracings of left-hind pugmarks on Pugmark Impression Pads (PIPs) - was largely superseded by camera trapping because track impressions deform across soil substrates and suffer from high observer and statistical bias.
questions.mini_lesson: In the Pugmark Census Method, field staff traced left-hind footprints on dusty Pugmark Impression Pads (PIPs) and tried to distinguish every individual tiger by subtle track dimensions. However, the same tiger leaves vastly different impressions in mud, loose sand, or hard clay, leading to double-counting and severe observer bias - problems solved by photographing invariant flank stripe patterns with camera traps.

questions.question: To convert standing dung-pile counts along forest transects into an estimate of absolute Asian elephant density, which two additional calibration rates must researchers measure?
options: Soil pH and tree canopy height
Annual rainfall and tiger stripe asymmetry
Average walking speed of elephants and tusk length
Daily defecation rate (dung piles produced per animal per day) and dung decay/disappearance rate
questions.transcript_quote: Converting indirect dung or pellet group counts into an absolute animal density estimate requires measuring two biological calibration rates: the daily defecation rate ($D$) and the dung decay or disappearance rate ($r$) in that specific season and habitat.
questions.mini_lesson: In dense rainforests where elephants or deer are rarely seen directly, researchers count dung piles along line transects. However, because dung accumulates based on how often animals defecate and vanishes based on how fast dung beetles, rain, and microbes break it down, converting dung density into animal density requires knowing both the daily defecation rate ($D$) and the local dung decay rate ($r$).

questions.question: Placing wildlife survey transects exclusively along paved tourist roads and easily accessible forest tracks introduces which type of error?
options: Equipment calibration bias
Convenience / roadside access sampling bias
Instrument resolution drift
Genetic outbreeding depression
questions.transcript_quote: Conducting wildlife surveys exclusively along convenient roadsides and tourist tracks introduces severe sampling (convenience/access) bias, over-representing edge-tolerant generalists while missing shy interior specialists.
questions.mini_lesson: Roadsides have altered microclimates, artificial clearings, vehicle noise, and human disturbance, meaning shy forest-interior species avoid them while edge-loving generalists (like spotted deer or macaques) may congregate along verges. Extrapolating roadside counts to the entire forest interior commits classic convenience/access sampling bias. Distractor (A) is a sibling bias term referring to faulty measuring gear.

questions.question: In monitoring large coastal ecosystems such as the Sundarbans, Mahanadi Delta, and Andaman Islands, satellite remote sensing (such as Landsat and Sentinel-2 NDVI mapping) is primarily used to:
options: Track mangrove canopy extent, vegetation health, dieback, and coastal land-use changes across landscape scales
Identify individual tigers by their flank stripes from space
Count underground earthworms in deep soil layers
Measure the body temperature of individual deep-sea whales
questions.transcript_quote: Satellite Earth observation using multispectral sensors (such as Landsat and Sentinel-2 NDVI mapping) enables landscape-scale monitoring of mangrove forest canopy cover, dieback, illegal embankment construction, and coastal carbon stocks across the Sundarbans, Mahanadi Delta, and Andaman Islands.
questions.mini_lesson: Muddy, tidal mangrove deltas like the Sundarbans are extremely difficult to traverse on foot, making optical and radar satellites ideal for tracking canopy vigour (via indices like NDVI), cyclone damage, aquaculture encroachment, and restoration progress across thousands of square kilometres. The distractors describe fine-scale individual animal measurements that satellites cannot perform.

questions.question: Beyond counting dung piles for abundance indices, how can fresh dung or scat samples be used to identify individual elusive animals without capturing them?
options: By painting the dung piles with UV-reflective yellow paint
By measuring the temperature of the dung pile three weeks later
By extracting host epithelial DNA shed onto the dung surface for non-invasive genetic mark-recapture
By burning the dung to measure hydrophobic soil formation
questions.transcript_quote: Fresh dung or scat samples slough off intestinal epithelial cells from the animal's gut lining, allowing researchers to extract host DNA (microsatellites) for non-invasive individual identification, sex determination, and genetic mark-recapture.
questions.mini_lesson: As food passes through an animal's digestive tract, a thin layer of intestinal lining cells coats the outer surface of the dung or scat. Swabbing fresh dung allows geneticists to amplify microsatellite DNA markers, identifying the exact individual animal, its sex, and its relatedness to others without ever darting or seeing it.

questions.question: What is the primary methodological risk of using Systematic Sampling (selecting every $k^{\text{th}}$ unit at a fixed spatial interval) across a natural landscape?
options: It requires complex computer random-number generators for every single point in the field
If the fixed sampling interval accidentally aligns with a repeating periodic feature in the landscape (such as parallel ridges and valleys), the sample becomes severely biased
It can never cover the entire geographic extent of a study area
It gives only the largest forest compartments a chance of being sampled
questions.transcript_quote: While systematic sampling (selecting every $k^{\text{th}}$ unit after a random start) ensures even spatial coverage and easy field navigation, its major risk is the periodic alignment trap: if the sampling interval coincides with a hidden periodic environmental pattern (such as parallel ridges and streams), estimates become severely biased.
questions.mini_lesson: Imagine placing vegetation plots every $500\text{ m}$ across a landscape where valleys and hilltops also repeat every $500\text{ m}$: every single plot might land exclusively on dry hilltops and miss the lush stream valleys entirely! This 'periodic alignment trap' is the classic vulnerability of systematic sampling. Distractor (D) describes PPS sampling.

questions.question: In standardized pan trapping for wild insect pollinators, why are shallow bowls painted in UV-reflective yellow, blue, and white and filled with water containing a drop of unscented soap?
options: The colours repel all birds and mammals while sterilizing the surrounding soil
The soap acts as a nutritional food reward so insects fly away heavier
The bowls are used to provide drinking water for large ungulates and carnivores
The colours mimic floral wavelengths to attract diverse pollinator guilds, and the soap breaks water surface tension so landing insects sink and are retained
questions.transcript_quote: Standardized pollinator pan trapping uses shallow bowls painted in UV-reflective yellow, blue, and white - placed at surrounding flower height - to attract different bee and fly guilds, filled with $1\%$ unscented soapy water where the surfactant lowers surface tension so trapped insects sink rather than walk on the water.
questions.mini_lesson: Different insect pollinator families have different colour preferences (for example, hoverflies and many bees favour yellow, while other wild bees prefer blue or white), so deploying a triad of yellow, blue, and white bowls at inflorescence height samples the full pollinator community. Adding a tiny drop of unscented detergent breaks the surface tension of the water so insects cannot skate off the surface and escape.

questions.question: In a Lincoln-Petersen capture-recapture study of pond turtles, researchers capture, mark, and release $M = 60$ turtles in Session 1. In Session 2, they capture a total of $n = 45$ turtles, of which $m = 15$ carry marks from Session 1. What is the estimated total population size ($N$)?
options: 90 turtles
120 turtles
180 turtles
675 turtles
questions.transcript_quote: Under the Lincoln-Petersen capture-recapture index, the proportion of marked animals in the second sample ($m / n$) equals the proportion of marked animals in the total population ($M / N$), giving the estimator $N = (M \cdot n) / m$.
questions.mini_lesson: Using the Lincoln-Petersen formula $N = (M \cdot n) / m$, multiply the number marked in Session 1 ($M = 60$) by the total captured in Session 2 ($n = 45$) and divide by the number of marked recaptures ($m = 15$): $N = (60 \times 45) / 15 = 2,700 / 15 = 180$ turtles. Intuitively, since $15/45 = 1/3$ of the second sample was marked, the $60$ marked turtles represent $1/3$ of the total pond population ($60 \times 3 = 180$).

questions.question: Which set correctly states the three core assumptions of the classical Lincoln-Petersen two-sample capture-recapture estimator?
options: The population is demographically closed, marks are not lost or overlooked, and marked and unmarked individuals have equal catchability
The population experiences rapid migration, marks fade within 24 hours, and only marked animals enter traps
The landscape is divided into habitat strata, larger plots are sampled more often, and no animals are released
All animals stand directly on the transect line, sighting angles are measured in degrees, and AIC is minimized
questions.transcript_quote: The classical Lincoln-Petersen estimator relies on three inviolate assumptions: (1) the population is demographically closed during the study; (2) marks are neither lost nor overlooked; and (3) every individual - marked or unmarked - has an equal probability of capture (equal catchability).
questions.mini_lesson: For the ratio $M / N = m / n$ to hold mathematically, the population size $N$ must not change between sessions (closed population), marked animals must remain recognizable (no tag loss), and being caught once must not make an animal easier or harder to catch in Session 2 (equal catchability). Distractor (D) lists assumptions/metrics of Line Transect Distance Sampling from Lecture 35.

questions.question: In a capture-recapture survey using food-baited traps, marked rodents learn that traps contain free food and become “trap-happy” (returning to traps much more frequently than unmarked rodents). How does this violate the Lincoln-Petersen model and bias the population estimate $N = (M \cdot n) / m$?
options: It reduces the number of marked recaptures ($m$), causing the formula to overestimate the true population size ($N$)
It inflates the number of marked recaptures ($m$), causing the formula to underestimate the true population size ($N$)
It increases the initial number of marked animals ($M$) before Session 1 begins
It has zero effect on the population estimate because food bait guarantees equal catchability
questions.transcript_quote: If marked animals become 'trap-happy' due to attractive bait, they are recaptured at an artificially high rate (inflating $m$ in the denominator of $N = M \cdot n / m$), which causes the Lincoln-Petersen estimator to underestimate true population size.
questions.mini_lesson: Look at the denominator of $N = (M \cdot n) / m$: when marked animals eagerly re-enter baited traps ('trap-happy'), the recapture count $m$ in the denominator becomes artificially large, which makes the calculated fraction $N$ artificially small (an underestimate of the true population). Conversely, 'trap-shy' animals avoid traps in Session 2, making $m$ too small and overestimating $N$ (Distractor B).

questions.question: What is a practical field drawback of Simple Random Sampling (SRS) when surveying a large, heterogeneous forest reserve?
options: It mathematically prohibits calculating a sample mean
It requires knowing the exact weight of every individual animal before selecting plots
It forces observers to sample only along paved highways
By pure random chance, selected units may cluster together in one part of the reserve, leaving large remote sectors or rare habitat types unsampled
questions.transcript_quote: Although Simple Random Sampling is statistically unbiased, in large heterogeneous landscapes random draws can accidentally cluster sample units in one area while leaving large sectors or rare habitats completely unvisited.
questions.mini_lesson: Because Simple Random Sampling picks units blindly with equal probability ($1/N$), a random draw of 20 plots might put 15 of them in one corner of the park and zero in a critical wetland valley. This spatial clumping increases travel cost and estimate variance across heterogeneous habitats - which is why managers upgrade to Stratified or Systematic designs.

questions.question: In Line Transect Distance Sampling, what is the fundamental assumption regarding detection on the transect centerline ($y = 0$)?
options: Zero animals are ever present on the transect centerline ($g(0) = 0$)
Animals located directly on the transect line ($y = 0$) are detected with 100% certainty ($g(0) = 1$)
Detection probability remains 100% constant out to an infinite perpendicular distance
Observers record only animals that flee before their initial position can be seen
questions.transcript_quote: The primary, foundational assumption of line transect distance sampling is that all individual animals located directly on the centerline of the transect (perpendicular distance $y = 0$) are detected with absolute $100\%$ certainty: $g(0) = 1$.
questions.mini_lesson: Distance sampling allows visibility $g(y)$ to drop off as perpendicular distance $y$ increases into thick forest, but to anchor the mathematical curve and calculate what fraction of animals was missed away from the line, detection right on the line itself ($y = 0$) must be $100\%$ ($g(0) = 1$). Distractor (C) describes a conventional strip transect where nothing is missed at any distance.

questions.question: When an observer walking a straight line transect spots a herd of spotted deer at a radial sighting distance $r$ and a sighting angle $\theta$ relative to the transect line, how is the perpendicular distance $y$ calculated?
options: $y = r \cdot \sin(\theta)$
$y = r / \tan(\theta)$
$y = r + \theta$
$y = r^2 \cdot \cos(\theta)$
questions.transcript_quote: In field line-transect surveys, observers measure the observer-to-animal radial sighting distance ($r$) with a rangefinder and the sighting angle ($\theta$) with a compass, calculating perpendicular distance from the transect line via right-triangle trigonometry as $y = r \cdot \sin(\theta)$.
questions.mini_lesson: Measuring perpendicular distance directly in the field requires leaving the transect line and crashing through bushes to the animal's spot. Instead, observers stay on the line, shoot the straight-line radial distance $r$ to the animal and the angle $\theta$ off the transect centerline, and use basic trigonometry ($y = r \cdot \sin(\theta)$, opposite side of the right triangle) to compute perpendicular distance.

questions.question: In distance sampling, what does the Effective Strip Half-Width ($\mu$ or ESHW) represent geometrically?
options: The total length of all roads inside a National Park
The minimum distance required between two camera-trap stations
The average body width of an adult herbivore
The perpendicular distance from the transect line at which the number of animals missed inside $\mu$ equals the number of animals detected beyond $\mu$
questions.transcript_quote: The Effective Strip Half-Width ($\mu = \int_0^w g(y)\,dy$) is the perpendicular distance from the transect centerline such that the number of unseen animals missed within distance $\mu$ exactly equals the number of seen animals detected beyond distance $\mu$.
questions.mini_lesson: Because detection $g(y)$ declines gradually with distance, distance sampling converts a curved detection profile into an equivalent rectangular 'effective strip' of half-width $\mu$. At distance $\mu$, the missed animals closer than $\mu$ are exactly balanced by the spotted animals farther than $\mu$, allowing density to be calculated simply as $\hat{D} = n / (2 \cdot L \cdot \mu)$.

questions.question: Using the distance sampling density formula $\hat{D} = \frac{n}{2 \cdot L \cdot \mu}$, what is the estimated density ($\hat{D}$) of sambar deer if observers detect $n = 80$ individual deer along a total transect length of $L = 20\text{ km}$ with an effective strip half-width of $\mu = 0.05\text{ km}$ ($50\text{ m}$)?
options: 20 deer per $\text{km}^2$
40 deer per $\text{km}^2$
80 deer per $\text{km}^2$
160 deer per $\text{km}^2$
questions.transcript_quote: Animal density in line-transect distance sampling is estimated by $\hat{D} = \frac{n}{2 \cdot L \cdot \mu}$, where $n$ is the number of animals detected, $L$ is total transect length, $\mu$ is the effective strip half-width, and $2 \cdot L \cdot \mu$ is the effective area surveyed on both sides of the line.
questions.mini_lesson: First, calculate the effective area surveyed on both sides of the $20\text{ km}$ transect: $\text{Effective Area} = 2 \cdot L \cdot \mu = 2 \times 20\text{ km} \times 0.05\text{ km} = 2.0\text{ km}^2$. Next, divide the $n = 80$ detected deer by the $2.0\text{ km}^2$ effective area: $\hat{D} = 80 / 2.0 = 40\text{ deer per km}^2$. Distractor (C) forgets the factor of $2$ (counting only one side of the transect line).

questions.question: How does dense forest undergrowth affect the detection function curve $g(y)$ compared to an open grassland, and how does distance sampling handle this difference?
options: Distance sampling ignores visibility differences and assumes identical strip widths in all habitats
Dense undergrowth makes $g(y)$ increase with distance so observers see farther in thickets than in grasslands
Dense undergrowth causes detection probability $g(y)$ to drop off more steeply with distance, yielding a smaller effective strip half-width ($\mu$) that mathematically corrects for lower visibility
Dense undergrowth prevents any mathematical model from being fitted
questions.transcript_quote: In dense vegetative cover, visibility drops off rapidly with perpendicular distance, causing a steeper detection curve $g(y)$ and a smaller effective strip half-width ($\mu$); distance sampling automatically corrects for this visibility bias by estimating $\mu$ separately for each habitat.
questions.mini_lesson: If you count 30 deer in an open meadow (where you can see 200 m) and 30 deer in a thick bamboo forest (where you can see only 25 m), raw counts would falsely suggest equal density. Distance sampling solves this visibility bias: the bamboo forest gets a much narrower effective strip half-width $\mu$ in the denominator of $\hat{D} = n / (2 \cdot L \cdot \mu)$, correctly revealing a much higher true density in the dense forest!

questions.question: In distance sampling analysis (such as Program DISTANCE), what is the role of the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)?
options: It selects the most parsimonious detection function model by balancing goodness-of-fit to the distance data against the number of model parameters
It tranquilizes large carnivores during collar fitting
It measures the battery voltage of underwater hydrophones
It calculates the genetic heterozygosity of a founder population
questions.transcript_quote: The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is an information-theoretic statistical metric used in distance sampling to compare candidate detection functions (such as half-normal, hazard-rate, or uniform) and select the most parsimonious model that balances goodness-of-fit against parameter complexity.
questions.mini_lesson: Adding extra mathematical parameters to a curve almost always makes it wiggle closer to sample points, but overfitting produces noisy, unreliable density estimates. The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) rewards models for fitting the observed distance histogram well while penalizing them for adding unnecessary parameters - so the candidate model with the lowest AIC score is chosen.

questions.question: Simple random sampling gives:
options: Larger units a higher chance of selection
Every sampling unit an equal chance of selection
Only remote areas a chance of selection
Every kth unit after a fixed start without randomness
questions.transcript_quote: In simple random sampling, every sampling unit in the target population has an equal, non-zero, and independent chance of being selected ($P = 1/N$).
questions.mini_lesson: Simple Random Sampling (SRS) is the foundational probability sampling design in which every unit in the sampling frame has an identical mathematical chance of being chosen. It works best in uniform landscapes, whereas distractor (A) defines Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) sampling and distractor (D) defines Systematic Sampling.

questions.question: Stratified sampling is especially useful when:
options: The whole landscape is uniform
Animal density varies across habitat types
Complete census is always possible
Sampling units cannot be mapped
questions.transcript_quote: Stratified random sampling partitions a heterogeneous landscape into non-overlapping homogeneous strata (such as riparian forest, grassland, and dry scrub) and is applied when animal density varies sharply across habitat types.
questions.mini_lesson: When wildlife density differs dramatically between habitats (for example, high deer density in grasslands versus low density in rocky scrub), Simple Random Sampling produces high variance and may miss rare habitats. Stratified sampling solves this by grouping the landscape into distinct habitat strata first and sampling randomly within each stratum. Distractor (A) describes the ideal condition for Simple Random Sampling, not stratified sampling.

questions.question: Which is an example of equipment bias?
options: Missed detections due to low observer skill
Faulty calibration of a measuring device
Dense vegetation hiding animals
Unrealistic movement assumptions in a model
questions.transcript_quote: Equipment bias is a systematic distortion in data collection resulting directly from the physical failure, drift, or faulty calibration of a measuring instrument, such as a miscalibrated laser rangefinder or faulty camera-trap sensor.
questions.mini_lesson: In wildlife monitoring, systematic bias is categorized by its source: equipment bias stems from defective or poorly calibrated instruments that consistently skew measurements in one direction. Distractor (A) is a classic sibling-term swap describing observer bias, (C) describes environmental visibility bias, and (D) describes mathematical model bias.

questions.question: Bias in wildlife monitoring means:
options: Random scatter around a true value
Systematic deviation from the true value
Higher cost of data collection
Larger sample size than required
questions.transcript_quote: Systematic bias is the consistent, directional deviation of a sample estimate from the true underlying population parameter, whereas imprecision is random scatter around the mean.
questions.mini_lesson: Bias (inaccuracy) means your survey method consistently overestimates or underestimates the true population size due to a structural flaw in design, equipment, or observer technique. Distractor (A) is the primary statistical trap: 'random scatter around a true value' defines imprecision (random error or variance), which cancels out with larger sample sizes, whereas systematic bias does not.

questions.question: In camera-trap based tiger estimation, individual tigers can be identified by:
options: Herd size
Nesting banks
Unique stripe patterns
Flowering season
questions.transcript_quote: Motion-triggered paired camera traps deployed along forest trails photograph passing tigers on both flanks, allowing researchers to identify individual Bengal tigers based on their unique, lifelong, asymmetrical stripe patterns.
questions.mini_lesson: Just like human fingerprints, the flank stripe patterns of Bengal tigers (and rosette patterns of leopards) are unique to each individual and remain unchanged throughout life. Paired camera traps capture both left and right flanks so software can match recaptures across space and time for mark-recapture density estimation. The distractors refer to ungulate social groups, crocodile/bird nesting, or plant phenology.

questions.question: Which pair represents losses from a population?
options: Natality and immigration
Births and recruitment
Mortality and emigration
Density and dispersal
questions.transcript_quote: In the basic population balancing equation $N_{t+1} = N_t + (B + I) - (D + E)$, the two demographic mechanisms that decrease population size (losses) are Deaths/Mortality ($D$) and Emigration ($E$).
questions.mini_lesson: A wildlife population loses individuals in only two ways: individuals die within the area (mortality/deaths) or individuals permanently leave the area to settle elsewhere (emigration). Distractor (A) 'Natality and immigration' is the exact opposite pole - the pair of demographic gains that add individuals to a population.

questions.question: A population in wildlife studies is best understood as which of the following?
options: All species living in a habitat during one season
Individuals of the same species in a defined area that are capable of interbreeding
All animals counted during a field survey
Individuals of different species using the same corridor
questions.transcript_quote: A population in wildlife studies is defined as a group of individuals of the same biological species occupying a defined geographical area at a given time that are capable of naturally interbreeding.
questions.mini_lesson: Three criteria define an ecological population: same species (conspecifics), shared spatial boundary (defined area), and reproductive connectivity (capable of interbreeding). Distractors (A) and (D) are sibling-level traps that describe multi-species 'communities' rather than a single-species population.

questions.question: Which pair represents gains to a population?
options: Births and immigration
Deaths and emigration
Births and deaths
Immigration and emigration
questions.transcript_quote: In the population balancing equation $N_{t+1} = N_t + (B + I) - (D + E)$, the two demographic mechanisms that increase population size (gains) are Births/Natality ($B$) and Immigration ($I$).
questions.mini_lesson: A population increases in size through two additive pathways: internal reproduction (births/natality) and external arrival of new individuals from outside patches (immigration). Distractor (B) lists the two population losses, while distractors (C) and (D) mix one gain with one loss to trap hurried readers.

questions.question: PPS sampling means:
options: Larger sampling units receive a higher chance of selection
Every unit has the same chance regardless of size
Only point transects are used
Animals are removed after each capture
questions.transcript_quote: Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) is a sampling design where larger sampling units - by geographical area, biomass, or volume - have a proportionally higher mathematical probability of being selected ($P_i \propto \text{Size}_i$).
questions.mini_lesson: When forest compartments, lakes, or watersheds vary hugely in area, giving tiny patches the same selection chance as massive blocks skews landscape estimates. Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) weights selection probability by unit size so larger units have a higher chance of being sampled. Distractor (B) defines Simple Random Sampling.

questions.question: Sampling intensity is calculated as:
options: Total animals divided by total area
Sample units divided by total population units
Marked animals divided by recaptured animals
Detection distance divided by transect length
questions.transcript_quote: Sampling intensity is the ratio of the number of sample units surveyed ($n$) to the total population units existing in the defined study universe ($N$): $\text{Sampling Intensity} = n / N$.
questions.mini_lesson: Sampling intensity measures what fraction of the total study area or total available compartments was actually surveyed by field teams ($n / N$, often expressed as a percentage). Distractor (A) is a formula swap that defines 'crude animal density', while (C) is a component of the Lincoln-Petersen capture-recapture ratio.

questions.question: In genetics, what does the term “genotype” refer to?
options: The outward physical appearance of an organism shaped only by weather
The underlying, heritable genetic and allelic constitution of an individual organism
The total number of species living in a geographic biome
The seasonal migration route learned from parent animals
questions.transcript_quote: Genotype is the underlying, internal genetic constitution - the specific set of alleles carried by an individual organism - whereas phenotype is the observable outward expression of traits.
questions.mini_lesson: While the phenotype is what you can observe or measure on the outside (coat colour, antler size, enzyme activity), the genotype is the hidden DNA blueprint - the specific pair of alleles (such as $RR$, $Rr$, or $rr$) an individual carries inside its cells. Distractor (A) confuses genotype with environmentally modified phenotype.

questions.question: When a homozygous red-flowered plant ($RR$) is crossed with a homozygous white-flowered plant ($rr$) and the resulting heterozygous offspring ($Rr$) produce uniformly pink flowers, which inheritance pattern is demonstrated?
options: Complete dominance
Codominance
Incomplete dominance
Chromosomal monosomy
questions.transcript_quote: Incomplete dominance occurs when the heterozygote displays an intermediate, blended phenotype halfway between the two homozygous parental traits - such as red and white parents producing pink offspring.
questions.mini_lesson: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is fully dominant over the other, so the heterozygote ($Rr$) produces an intermediate blended trait (pink) between the two homozygous extremes (red and white). Distractor (B) 'Codominance' is the primary trap: in codominance, both alleles are expressed separately at full strength (which would produce flowers with distinct red and white patches, not blended pink).

questions.question: In chromosomes, long negatively charged DNA molecules are tightly coiled and packaged around spool-like structural proteins called:
options: Histones
Myoglobins
Neurotransmitters
Phthalates
questions.transcript_quote: Chromosomes are filamentous cellular structures formed by long DNA molecules tightly wrapped around structural histone proteins, allowing metres of genetic code to fit inside a microscopic cell nucleus.
questions.mini_lesson: To pack billions of DNA base pairs into a microscopic nucleus without tangling or breaking them during cell division, eukaryotic cells wind DNA around positively charged protein spools called histones to form chromatin and chromosomes. Distractor (B) is a muscle oxygen-binding protein (from Week 11 capture myopathy), and (D) is a plasticizer additive.

questions.question: An individual organism that carries two different alleles at a specific gene locus (such as $Rr$) is described as:
options: Homozygous dominant
Heterozygous
Homozygous recessive
Haploid
questions.transcript_quote: In a diploid organism, an individual carrying two identical alleles at a locus ($RR$ or $rr$) is homozygous, whereas an individual carrying two different alleles ($Rr$) is heterozygous.
questions.mini_lesson: Diploid organisms inherit two copies of each gene - one from each parent. If both copies are the same version ($RR$ or $rr$), the individual is homozygous; if the two copies are different versions ($Rr$), the individual is heterozygous. Maintaining high heterozygosity across a wild population is a primary goal of conservation genetics.

questions.question: Why can two organisms with the exact same genotype occasionally exhibit noticeable differences in their observable phenotype (such as body weight or plant height)?
options: Alleles are inherited only from the environment and never from parents
Genotype has zero influence on any biological trait
Chromosomes randomly dissolve whenever an animal changes habitats
Phenotype is shaped by the interaction between an organism's genotype and its environment (nutrition, temperature, stress)
questions.transcript_quote: An organism's observable phenotype is not determined by its genotype in isolation; rather, $\text{Phenotype} = \text{Genotype} + \text{Environment}$ (plus genotype-by-environment interactions).
questions.mini_lesson: While genes set the developmental potential of an organism, environmental factors - such as diet quality, temperature, sunlight, disease, and stress - shape how those genes are expressed into physical traits. Two genetically identical twin fawns raised on lush forage versus drought-stricken scrub will develop very different adult body weights.

questions.question: How can non-invasive molecular genetic tools assist wildlife law enforcement and anti-poaching operations?
options: By converting synthetic plastic into living animal tissue
By automatically arresting poachers using satellite lasers
By identifying the exact species, geographic population of origin, and individual identity from confiscated ivory, horn, skin, or bushmeat samples
By replacing all field forest guards with laboratory microscopes
questions.transcript_quote: In wildlife forensics, conservation genetics allows authorities to extract DNA from seized blood, smoked bushmeat, ivory, or skins to prove species identity, pinpoint the geographic reserve of origin, and link separated body parts to a single poached carcass.
questions.mini_lesson: Poachers frequently disguise illegal bushmeat by smoking or mincing it, removing external morphological features. Forensic DNA barcoding and microsatellite profiling allow wildlife crime labs to prove in court that a seized piece of meat or horn came from a protected Schedule I species and even trace which specific population or reserve it was poached from.

questions.question: In a diploid wildlife population of $1,000$ individuals ($2,000$ total gene copies at the $R$ locus), genetic testing reveals $640$ homozygous dominant ($RR$) individuals, $320$ heterozygous ($Rr$) individuals, and $40$ homozygous recessive ($rr$) individuals. What is the allele frequency ($p$) of the $R$ allele?
